units.t: Prehistoric Life. Episode one.
In this episode: The first life on Earth, Fossils and Dinosaurs: rulers of the Mesozoic.
Part one. The first life on Earth.
Some of the oldest evidence of life on Earth is in Western Australia, and you can still see its living relatives at Shark Bay.
A hostile young planet.
Earth formed about 4.
54 billion years ago from dust and rock orbiting the young Sun.
Early on, a Mars-sized body is thought to have smashed into it, flinging out the debris that became the Moon.
The surface was bombarded by space rocks and the air had no oxygen.
Yet it may have cooled faster than once thought.
Tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia, about 4.
4 billion years old, are the oldest known pieces of Earth, and their chemistry suggests liquid water, perhaps even oceans, existed remarkably early.
How life began.
How non-living chemistry became life is a great open question.
In 1952, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey passed sparks through gases and water and made amino acids, showing life's ingredients can form naturally.
Leading ideas include deep-sea hydrothermal vents and shallow ponds that dry out and refill, concentrating chemicals, an echo of Darwin's 'warm little pond'.
Many researchers think early life used RNA, which can both store information and speed up reactions, before DNA and proteins took over.
All living things share the same basic genetic code, pointing to LUCA, the last universal common ancestor.
It wasn't the first life, but the population all survivors descend from, probably single-celled microbes in a warm, oxygen-free place.
One 2024 study estimated about 4.
2 billion years ago; the timing is debated.
Oldest evidence.
Some of the oldest widely accepted evidence of life comes from the Pilbara in Western Australia.
Rocks about 3.
5 billion years old contain stromatolites, layered structures built by microbial communities, and the 3.
4 billion-year-old stromatolites at Strelley Pool are well studied.
Older claims exist, including possible 3.
7 billion-year-old stromatolites in Greenland, but they are contested because non-living processes can mimic life.
You can see living stromatolites at Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay, a World Heritage Area.
The water is about twice as salty as seawater, which keeps away snails and other grazers.
Microbial mats trap and bind sediment into domes, often growing a fraction of a millimetre a year.
Some are thought to be a few thousand years old.
They offer a glimpse of what coastlines may have looked like for much of Earth's history.
The oxygen revolution.
For its first two billion years, Earth's air had almost no oxygen.
That changed when cyanobacteria began photosynthesising, using sunlight to split water and releasing oxygen as waste.
At first the oxygen was absorbed by iron dissolved in the oceans, which rusted and settled to form banded iron formations.
The Pilbara's huge iron-ore deposits in the Hamersley Range formed in this era, so Australia's iron exports partly owe their existence to ancient microbes.
Around 2.
4 billion years ago, oxygen began building up in the atmosphere, an event called the Great Oxidation Event.
It was toxic to many microbes but opened the way for complex life.
Complex cells to animals.
The complex cell, or eukaryote, has a nucleus and internal compartments, and plants, animals and fungi are all built from them.
A key event was when one microbe engulfed another without digesting it, and the swallowed partner became the mitochondrion, the cell's power station.
Plants gained chloroplasts by absorbing cyanobacteria.
This idea, endosymbiosis, was championed by Lynn Margulis in the 1960s and is widely accepted.
Complex cells appear in the fossil record at least 1.
6 billion years ago.
Soft-bodied multicellular life appeared in the Ediacaran from about 635 million years ago.
From around 538 million years ago, most major animal groups appear within perhaps 20 million years, the Cambrian explosion, bringing eyes, shells, legs and jaws.
Sites include the Emu Bay Shale on Kangaroo Island.
The key idea: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, yet zircon crystals from Western Australia suggest liquid water existed within a few hundred million years.
Part two. Fossils.
Almost nothing that dies becomes a fossil.
The few that do are messages from deep time, and Australia holds some of the most important.
A rare event.
Most living things vanish after death.
Scavengers eat them, bacteria break them down and weather scatters the rest.
To become a fossil, an organism usually needs to be buried quickly in mud, sand, volcanic ash or sediment, which cuts off oxygen and scavengers.
Hard parts such as bones, teeth and shells survive best, so the record is dominated by shelled sea creatures.
Only a tiny fraction of all species are thought to be preserved, mostly those living in or near water where sediment builds up.
Gaps are expected, not suspicious, and predictions still work: in 2004, researchers searched rocks of the right age and found Tiktaalik, a transitional fish with limb-like fins.
Bone to stone, and traces.
Once buried, minerals such as silica or calcite can seep into bone or wood and gradually turn it to stone, keeping fine detail.
Sometimes the original dissolves, leaving a mould that fills to form a cast.
Soft tissue is rare: insects in amber, mammoths in Siberian permafrost, animals in tar pits.
Trace fossils record behaviour instead of bodies: footprints, burrows, bite marks, nests and coprolites, the polite name for fossilised dung.
They can show how fast an animal moved or what it ate.
At Lark Quarry near Winton, Queensland, thousands of dinosaur footprints about 95 million years old were once read as a stampede.
Some researchers now think the animals were wading or swimming.
Dating fossils.
Scientists date fossils in two main ways.
Relative dating uses superposition: in undisturbed layers, deeper rock is older.
Widespread index fossils help match layers across regions.
For actual ages, scientists use radiometric dating, measuring the steady decay of radioactive elements such as uranium or potassium in volcanic ash layers above and below a fossil.
A common myth is that dinosaurs are carbon dated.
Radiocarbon dating only works back to about 50,000 years, so it suits mammoths and early human sites, not dinosaurs.
Finds that changed science.
In the early 1800s, Mary Anning, a working-class woman from Lyme Regis in England, found the first ichthyosaur skeleton to be recognised scientifically and one of the first plesiosaurs.
Her finds helped establish that extinction was real, yet she was largely denied credit in her lifetime.
Megalosaurus, 1824, and Iguanodon, 1825, were the first dinosaurs named, and early reconstructions got a lot wrong: Iguanodon's thumb spike was first placed on its nose like a rhino's horn.
In 1946, geologist Reg Sprigg noticed strange impressions in the Ediacara Hills of the Flinders Ranges.
They were soft-bodied sea-floor creatures over 550 million years old, among the oldest large, complex life known.
The Ediacaran period, named in 2004, was the first new geological period in over a century.
Finding fossils yourself.
Fossil hunting can be a rewarding hobby, but rules matter.
Collecting is generally banned in national parks and many protected sites, and important fossils, such as those at Ediacara, are protected by law.
Rules vary between states, so check before you dig, and always get landholder permission on private land.
If you find something that looks significant, photograph it where it lies, note the location and contact your state museum.
Many major Australian finds, including dinosaurs around Winton, were first spotted by farmers and members of the public.
Museum fossil days and guided digs are a great way to start.
The key idea: Fossilisation is rare: an organism usually needs quick burial, so the record favours hard parts and watery places.
Part three. Dinosaurs: rulers of the Mesozoic.
They dominated the land for over 150 million years, left thousands of footprints in outback Queensland, and one branch of the family still visits your backyard.
What counts as a dinosaur.
Richard Owen coined 'dinosaur', meaning 'terrible lizard', in 1842.
Scientifically, dinosaurs are reptiles that walked with their legs held straight beneath the body, not sprawled to the side like a lizard.
That rules out pterosaurs, flying reptiles, marine reptiles such as plesiosaurs and mosasaurs, and the sail-backed Dimetrodon, which was closer to mammal ancestors.
They lived through the Mesozoic Era.
The Triassic, 252 to 201 million years ago, saw the first small dinosaurs around 230 million years ago.
The Jurassic brought giant sauropods and Stegosaurus.
The Cretaceous, ending 66 million years ago, gave us Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops.
T.
rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.
Branches and real sizes.
Since the 1880s, scientists have sorted dinosaurs by hip shape.
The lizard-hipped saurischians include meat-eating theropods like Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor, and huge plant-eating sauropods like Brachiosaurus.
The bird-hipped ornithischians were plant-eaters such as Triceratops, Stegosaurus and duck-billed hadrosaurs.
Confusingly, birds evolved from the lizard-hipped branch.
Some researchers propose redrawing this tree, but museums still use the two-branch system.
T.
rex reached about 12 metres and perhaps 8 tonnes.
Argentinosaurus may have been 30 metres or more and 60 tonnes, though estimates vary.
The real Velociraptor, from Mongolia, was turkey-sized and feathered.
More than 1,000 non-bird species have been named.
Birds are dinosaurs.
In 1861, quarry workers in Germany found Archaeopteryx, a roughly 150-million-year-old animal with feathered wings but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail.
It hinted at a link between dinosaurs and birds.
Since the 1990s, discoveries in north-eastern China have revealed dozens of feathered dinosaurs, many unable to fly.
Birds share wishbones, hollow bones and egg-brooding behaviour with theropods like Velociraptor.
Scientists now agree that birds are a branch of the dinosaur family tree.
That makes the magpie on your fence, and the emu and cassowary, living dinosaurs.
Australia's dinosaur country.
Australian fossils are rarer than North America's, but discoveries keep coming.
Around Winton, rocks about 95 million years old have yielded the sauropods Diamantinasaurus and Savannasaurus and the predator Australovenator, nicknamed 'Banjo'.
In 2021, scientists described Australotitan from near Eromanga, estimated at 25 to 30 metres long.
Muttaburrasaurus and the armoured Kunbarrasaurus are Queensland finds too.
At Lark Quarry, more than 3,000 small footprints were long read as a stampede, though some researchers now argue the dinosaurs were wading.
In Victoria, Dinosaur Cove yielded Leaellynasaura.
About 110 million years ago, Australia was joined to Antarctica, inside the polar circle, so these dinosaurs coped with months of winter darkness.
Common myths.
Popular culture gets a lot wrong.
Humans and non-bird dinosaurs never met: the last of them died about 66 million years before our species appeared.
Most dinosaurs were not giants; many were dog-sized or smaller.
The old image of sluggish, cold-blooded creatures dragging their tails has been replaced by active, fast-growing animals, many with feathers, though their metabolism is still researched.
Nor were they failures.
Dinosaurs thrived for more than 150 million years and, through birds, are still here.
Next time you visit a museum, look for feathers, posture and scale, and you will see how far the science has moved.
The key idea: Dinosaurs are a specific group of land reptiles that walked with legs straight under the body, and they lived through the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous until 66 million years ago.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do the Jack Hills zircons suggest about the young Earth?
Answer. Liquid water existed surprisingly early.
Question two. What usually has to happen for an organism to become a fossil?
Answer. It is buried quickly, shutting out oxygen.
Question three. Which of these was a true dinosaur?
Answer. Triceratops.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
